analysis.one_liner: Created a government-run health insurance program covering every U.S. resident, replacing Medicare, Medicaid, and private duplicate coverage.
analysis.headline: The universal health care bill was sent to four House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, the federal employee health program, and military dependent coverage with a single government-run health plan covering every U.S. citizen and lawful resident. It would have banned deductibles and copayments for most care, barred doctors from billing patients extra, and outlawed private insurance that duplicates the public plan. It would have been funded by a new payroll tax on employers, a health care income tax, and higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident — the roughly 38 million Americans uninsured at the time, plus everyone whose employer coverage had high deductibles, exclusions, or pre-existing condition denials. Coverage would be portable from job to job and state to state, automatic at birth, and include dental, mental health, prescription drugs, and long-term care.

how_it_helps.text: Entitles every U.S. citizen and lawful resident to comprehensive coverage including hospital care, prescription drugs, dental, mental health, hospice, and home and community-based long-term care, with no deductibles, coinsurance, or copayments for acute and preventive care [S2][S3].

Prohibits providers from balance-billing patients for covered services and bars the sale of private insurance that duplicates the public plan, eliminating premium and out-of-pocket costs for covered care [S2][S3].

Replaces Medicare, Medicaid, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and CHAMPUS after December 31, 2002, so coverage follows the person rather than the job or age, with automatic enrollment at birth and portability across states [S2][S3].

Pays hospitals through approved global budgets and doctors through a fee schedule, removing the insurance-claim overhead and uncompensated-care burden that hospitals currently shift onto paying patients [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay a new payroll tax, higher-income households a new health care income tax, and smokers higher tobacco excise taxes; health insurers would lose the market for duplicate coverage, and hospitals and drug makers would lose the ability to bill market rates. Providers no longer facing uninsured patients' unpaid bills would give up some of that back.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises substantial new taxes: a payroll tax on employers, a health care income tax, and increased excise taxes on tobacco products to fill the American Health Security Trust Fund [S3].

It would end Medicare, Medicaid, and federal employee health benefits as they exist and ban duplicative private insurance, so people satisfied with current coverage would lose it and the transition would disrupt coverage for tens of millions [S2][S3].
Long-term care is not free: home and community-based services carry 20% coinsurance and nursing facility care 35%, waived only for people near the poverty line [S3].

Hospitals would operate under government-approved global budgets and doctors under a set fee schedule with no balance billing, and a national board would decide payment rates and covered services — trading provider payment flexibility and patient choice of add-on coverage for cost control [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered universal coverage with no out-of-pocket costs for most care, paid for by broad new taxes that would fall on employers, high earners, and smokers. The trade-off is real: everyone would lose private coverage that duplicates the public plan, and the transition away from Medicare, Medicaid, and employer plans would be the largest reorganization of American health care ever attempted. Whether the trust fund taxes would have fully covered the cost of benefits is not established in the bill's record.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four committees in March 2001, shuffled to subcommittees, and no committee ever reported it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the American Health Security Act on March 22, 2001, with 23 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform, and Armed Services Committees, and then to the Health, Military Personnel, and Civil Service subcommittees [S5].
No committee held a markup or reported the bill; the only further activity in the record was the sponsor's introductory remarks in May 2002 [S5].
The bill gathered 28 cosponsors — 27 of 208 House Democrats and the chamber's sole Independent — and no Republicans [S4].
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and all legislation not passed died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept the private coverage market intact, and employers, hospitals, and drug makers avoided the new taxes and government-set payment rates. Americans without adequate coverage gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers kept the status quo

industries.note: The bill bans the sale of private insurance that duplicates the public plan, effectively ending private health coverage for services the program covers. Insurers' revenue depends on charging premiums for coverage the bill would provide without premiums, so their interest runs against the public's here.

The bill covers outpatient prescription drugs for everyone, expanding the paying customer base, but a national board sets drug payment rates, ending the ability to negotiate per-patient prices with multiple insurers. Higher drug prices are a cost the public bears, so the industry's pricing interest conflicts with patients' here.

Hospitals would be paid from government-approved global budgets — predictable revenue and an end to uncompensated emergency care — but likely below what they charge insured patients today. Patients would stop absorbing those charges as cost-shifting.

Doctors would get guaranteed payment with no insurer denials and no patient billing, but under a set fee schedule, mandatory assignment, and a ban on balance billing. Private-practice flexibility would narrow.

Employers would owe a new payroll tax but would stop paying health insurance premiums for workers, and could still offer extra benefits voluntarily. The net effect depends on the tax level relative to current premiums, which the record does not specify.
